column2: I’m trying to understand what tokenized stocks actually mean. Where does the value come from? A stock is an actual percentage of a company’s ownership. A token of a stock is basically an NFT of a stock? The value is only from what other people are willing to pay for it?

Company A will accept funds to buy some stock like MSFT, then they will mint a token i.e. xMSFT that you'll own in a blockchain ledger. You can trade this for whatever you want but the company promises to buy any token xMSFT at MSFT price whenever you want[1]. So the tokenized asset remains pegged as long as there's trust in the institution.

Also, the company will grow a balance sheet out of the funds created by the owners of the tokens and they frequently will give you some sort of yield on your position.

[1] Open Market hours and usually accompanied by a fee.

The ultimate goal of tokenized stocks is that the token is a share - just represented on the public blockchain instead of in the databases of companies like Fidelity. So in this respect, it's just changing the record keeping system. We're not quite there yet, but that's the vision.

Why would you do this? Current stock trading often takes a day or so to actually settle - you execute a buy but it doesn't settle immediately. There is room for leverage and counter-party risk to live in that gap.

Tokenized stocks (or any asset) is building towards atomic on-chain settlement - you have stock in MSFT, I have stablecoins, we perform an atomic transfer where you send me MSF and I send you stablecoins. This speeds up the system and eliminates counterparty risk. We each must have the asset ready to trade at this point in time.

The benefit is faster settlement, not keeping capital locked up because of long settlement times and decreasing the space where leverage and counter-party risk can live.

Longer term - this potentially means it could be easier for non-US parties to buy US stocks. I can put my savings in the stock market, but a farmer in a developing country cannot. But with tokenized shares, they could invest in US equities - or even a fraction of a US equity if they cannot afford a full share. So this longer term vision could democratize global access to capital markets.

Somehow every time I try to make this argument about stock buybacks, some people vigorously defend them as not just somehow a glorified Ponzi scheme.

Why would you see them as a Ponzi scheme?

The cash for buybacks comes from company operations, which they give to investors in exchange for destroying the outstanding security. The cash for Ponzi schemes comes from other investors, which they receive in exchange for issuing more securities and use to fund investors who want to cash out. They are in many ways opposites.

> The cash for Ponzi schemes comes from other investors, which they receive in exchange for issuing more securities and use to fund investors who want to cash out.

If the value of something is only "someone else will pay for it, and then later they will sell it", that to me is effectively the same as a Ponzi scheme. There's no inherent value in the actual thing being bought and sold other than the buying and selling of it. Maybe calling them "Pokemon cards for companies" would be a better way of describing why I find it nonsensical to claim there's any real link between the company and the stock unit when buybacks are the only way to make money off them.

Ponzi scheme has a very specific definition, which is that the money to pay out earlier investors comes from new investors. That's specifically the test that the FTC and SEC use to prosecute such cases. With buybacks, the money used to buy out investors comes from the operating profits of the company. Economic activity is happening, money is being exchanged for goods and services, and then the money is being returned to shareholders in accordance with the company's fiduciary duties.

Curious if you understand where the cash from a buyback comes from? That it's out of the corporate treasury, where it was previously accounted for as part of the profits of the corporation?

I can't tell if you're being condescending intentionally or not, but I'm not sure how you could get the impression that I don't understand what "buyback" means. Obviously it comes from the company; otherwise it's just a regular stock sale that doesn't need any additional descriptor.

The issue to me is that the division between "money companies get from selling their shares" and "money companies get from selling their products" is artificial; whether it gets taxed differently is a procedural issue, not something that inherently defines what "value" is. When the value of something is only from selling it again in the future, it's inherently only valuable as long as there's someone else to pass it onto to sell it again later. Sticking the company in the middle of passing it along doesn't magically change whether it's sensible or not. That's what I mean by "effectively a Ponzi scheme", even if it's not strictly one in the definitional sense. The same arguments for why a Ponzi scheme is undesirable apply.

I'm condescending to everyone; my wife, when we first started dating, was like "He doesn't mean to be condescending, but, well, he is."

> Obviously it comes from the company; otherwise it's just a regular stock sale that doesn't need any additional descriptor.

This is incorrect. A buyback is when a company buys its stock. It is giving cash to shareholders, and taking the shares back. A stock sale is the opposite, when the company sells its stock and receives money from the new shareholders. The direction of cash flow is very important here, because a key difference between a Ponzi scheme and a buyback is that in a buyback, the company is distributing cash to investors, not taking cash in.

> The issue to me is that the division between "money companies get from selling their shares" and "money companies get from selling their products" is artificial

If you're collapsing these two, you're generalizing beyond the point of usefulness, and ignoring all of the reasons why people engage in economic activity in the first place.

There are many, many industries where the consumer does not even get to sell the object again in the future. When you go out to a restaurant, the meal disappears within an hour, leaving you with just memories and indigestion. When you go to an amusement park, you have fun while you're there and leave with nothing. When you pay rent, you have a roof over your head for the month and then nothing afterwards. When you go to a casino, you get your hopes and excitement up while you're there and leave with less than nothing. When you buy alcohol or tobacco, you're spending money on the privilege of poisoning yourself.

Almost everyone would consider these legitimate economic exchanges, though. They may be inadvisable on a time-preference basis because your money disappears and you end up with nothing durable in return, but few people would argue that a large part of our economy is made up of transactions like this.

You're right though that you can take the corporation out of the equation and they still make just as much sense. If you take the corporation, its accounting statements, and the corporate treasury out of the equation, then a buyback is taking money earned from providing goods and services, and distributing it to the shareholders. The difference from a dividend is which shareholders receive the distribution: in a dividend it is distributed equally across all shareholders (who continue to remain shareholders), while in a buyback it distributes the cash to the people who least want to own the business in the future, paying them out entirely and distributing future profits to a smaller set of shareholders.

> This is incorrect. A buyback is when a company buys its stock. It is giving cash to shareholders, and taking the shares back
